newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan prosecutors arrest DKB vice president.
newsitem.headline: Japan prosecutors arrest DKB vice president.

text.p: Prosecutors on Friday arrested Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB) vice president Ichiro Fujita, who was once briefly appointed to head the bank, and another executive on suspicion of making illegal loans to a racketeer.
Friday's arrests brought to 10 the number of DKB officials apprehended in connection with the payoff scandal involving "sokaiya", racketeers who threaten to disrupt shareholder meetings.

The scandal also involves Japan's biggest brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd, where five people including a vice president have been arrested. The racketeer at the heart of the affair has also been arrested.

On Tuesday, four former DKB executives were arrested on suspicion of making illicit loans to a racketeer, and half of the 40 board members at DKB, one of Japan's leading commercial banks, resigned in a shakeup which included the naming of a new president.

Prosecutors have said their investigations into all the DKB officials involve 39 separate loans, totalling 8.8 billion yen ($77.1 million), which were believed to have been made through Daiwa Shinyo, a non-bank financial firm affiliated with DKB.
When the scandal first ensnared DKB last month, the bank's president Katsuhiko Kondo stepped down and Fujita was briefly appointed to replace him.

But several weeks later Fujita also fell from grace when outrage grew at his admission that he knew of the questionable loans which DKB said were made to Yoshinori Koike, the younger brother of Ryuichi Koike, the "sokaiya" racketeer at the heart of the scandal.
DKB on Tuesday appointed managing director Katsuyuki Sugita, 54, as president.
The scandal is unfolding just as Japan kicks off its "Big Bang" reforms of its long-protected financial sector -- a fact which has made authorities keen to take a tough stance.

DKB, which like Nomura is suffering customer defections and faces possible stiff administrative penalties over the scandal, has said it will implement management reforms to prevent any future misdeeds, including the creation of a committee of outside auditors to check for dubious business activities.
The Commercial Code bans payoffs to sokaiya, who extort money by threatening to disrupt shareholders meetings.
